To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we used mass spectrometry to identify cellular proteins that interact with HCV E2, and that we identified a new host factor UGT1 that regulates HCV replication.
we have identified 85 cellular proteins that interact with HCV E2 and that we have validated three of these interactions.

1) We have identified novel E2 interacting proteins in HCV infected human liver cells; 2) We demonstrated that UGT1 plays an important role during the HCV lifecycle; 3) We showed that the transmembrane domain is important for the interaction between E2 and NS4B.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for identifying and characterizing novel viral-host interactions in human liver cells infected with HCV.

the study of the interaction between hepatitis C virus (HIV) and human hepatocytes, and the results obtained will help to further understand the pathogenesis of HIV infection and the mechanism of HIV entry into cells.
the interaction of HCV E2 with cellular proteins in the host cell.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the E2 complex is a dynamic and complex protein network that includes a large number of host and viral proteins.
this study identified novel E2 binding proteins in HCV infected cells and provided new insight into HCV infection and pathogenesis.
the proteomics study has provided new insight into the understanding of HCV biology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have successfully purified HCV E2 complex formed during virus infection and identified a number of novel binding partners for HCV E2.
we have successfully identified a number of novel E2 binding proteins in HCV-infeceted hepatoma cells, among which UGT1 was further validated and shown to be a negative regulator of HCV production.
we have identified a number of novel host factors that interact with HCV E2 and some of the host factors are critical for the viral lifecycle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HCV E1 and E2 form a heterodimer on the virus envelope and that the E1-E2 heterodimer interacts with NS4B and NS5B.
we have identified novel HCV-host interactions, which will help us understand how HCV infects human cells.
HCV E1 and E2 proteins are not only involved in viral entry, but also play important roles in virus morphogenesis.
